summary: Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) finds paths through NATs using candidate addresses and STUN checks. This RFC extends ICE to support TCP candidates, so media can be sent over TCP when UDP will not work.

eli5.summary: Two people looking for a way to connect try many doors. This adds one more kind of door, so they can connect even when the usual one is locked.

questions: why does ice use rfc 4571 framing
subtitle: How ICE finds a path through NATs when media has to travel over TCP, alone or as a fallback to UDP.

tldr.problem: ICE only defines UDP candidates, but some media protocols run only over TCP, and some networks block UDP while allowing TCP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6544 adds active, passive and simultaneous-open TCP candidates, a new tcptype attribute in SDP, and rules for running STUN checks over TCP with RFC 4571 framing.
tldr.outcome: Agents can offer UDP and TCP candidates together, prefer UDP, and fall back to TCP, although ICE over TCP is generally less efficient than over UDP.

facts.label: Max outstanding attempts
facts.value: 5 per peer IP address (SHOULD NOT exceed)

today: RFC 6544 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends ICE as defined in RFC 5245.

sections.title: Why ICE Needs TCP Candidates
sections.content:
Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE, RFC 5245) helps two agents behind NATs find a working path by trying candidate transport addresses with STUN-based connectivity checks. It only defines procedures for UDP.

The RFC gives two reasons to add TCP. Some media protocols run only over TCP, for example screen sharing and instant messaging. And in some networks, overly restrictive NAT and firewall devices block UDP altogether while general TCP is permitted. With this extension an agent can gather UDP and TCP candidates, list the UDP ones with higher priority, and use TCP only if UDP fails.

It is particularly useful with TURN: an agent makes an outbound TCP connection to a relay on the public network, which works broadly through NATs and firewalls. The base behavior of ICE is unchanged except for the extensions in this document.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the usual way to talk is blocked. This lets the computers try a slower but more widely open way as a backup.

sections.title: Active, Passive and Simultaneous-Open Candidates
sections.content:
TCP candidates come in three kinds. An active candidate is one the agent will use to open an outbound connection but never to receive one. A passive candidate receives incoming connection attempts but does not make any. A simultaneous-open (S-O) candidate is one where the agent tries to connect at the same time as its peer.

Active candidates carry an IP address and a port, but the port is meaningless and ignored by the peer, so they need not be physically allocated during gathering. When candidates are paired, active pairs with passive, and S-O pairs with S-O. Everything else about check lists and the Valid list works as for UDP.

Because TCP is a byte stream, STUN messages need framing. TCP media streams using ICE use the framing from RFC 4571, even when the application protocol is not RTP. (D)TLS also runs over that shim, and STUN stays outside the (D)TLS connection.
sections.eli5: One side knocks on the door, the other waits behind it, or both knock at the same time and hope the door opens in the middle.

sections.title: Gathering, Prioritizing and Encoding Candidates
sections.content:
Agents SHOULD be configurable to obtain or not obtain TCP candidates, because some providers prefer no media to media over TCP. Gathering follows a set order: host candidates, then server reflexive, NAT-assisted and UDP-tunneled candidates, then passive (and possibly S-O) relayed candidates. The agent MUST keep gathered TCP connections open until ICE processing completes. For each component on each interface, an agent SHOULD obtain two host candidates on different ports, one S-O and one passive, plus an active placeholder.

Priority uses the ICE formula, with the local preference extended to include direction: (2^13) * direction-pref + other-pref. Direction-pref is between 0 and 7, other-pref between 0 and 8191. For host, UDP-tunneled and relayed candidates the recommended direction preferences are 6 for active, 4 for passive and 2 for S-O. For NAT-assisted and server reflexive candidates they are 6 for S-O, 4 for active and 2 for passive. The recommended type preferences for the new types are 105 for NAT-assisted and 75 for UDP-tunneled. For RTP, UDP candidates SHOULD be preferred over TCP.

In SDP, TCP candidates use the transport token TCP and a new tcptype extension with the value active, passive or so. Active candidates MUST use port 9 (Discard). If the default candidate is TCP, the agent MUST include the a=setup and a=connection attributes from RFC 4145.

Lite agents, which always have a public, globally unique IP address, gather only passive host candidates for TCP unless active ones are needed as defaults.
sections.eli5: Each side makes a list of ways to be reached, ranks them with the best first, and writes them in a message with a label for which kind each one is.

sections.title: Ways to Collect Candidates
sections.content:
Only host candidates are mandatory to think about; the other techniques are optional. To get a reasonable success ratio, an implementation SHOULD support at least one relayed technique (such as TURN) and one technique for discovering the NAT-given address (such as STUN). Both IPv4 and IPv6 candidates should be gathered.

  • Host: open TCP sockets on the interfaces. Most efficient with no NATs between hosts, but usually fails behind different NATs.
  • Server reflexive: ask a server on the other side of the NAT for the mapped address, for example with STUN.
  • NAT-assisted: talk to the NAT directly, for example with UPnP IGD or NAT-PMP, so the NAT can adjust its behavior.
  • UDP-tunneled: wrap TCP in UDP, such as with Teredo, trading extra overhead for simpler traversal.
  • Relayed: use a relay such as TURN TCP. It works with all existing NATs but gives a sub-optimal path and burdens the relay, so it is often the last resort.

Offering too many candidates makes large check lists and long-lasting checks, so using several techniques that produce redundant candidates is discouraged.
sections.eli5: There are several tricks for finding a path, from simple to clever. A helper in the middle always works but is slowest, so it is the last choice.

sections.title: Connectivity Checks and Connection Management
sections.content:
TCP and UDP pairs share one check list and are checked in priority order, but only by full implementations. To check a TCP pair, the agent opens a connection for the pair's 5-tuple if none exists, then sends STUN Binding requests inside RFC 4571 frames. If the connection cannot be opened, the pair is marked Failed. Retransmissions are not needed because TCP delivers reliably. Passive and S-O candidates MUST accept incoming connections.

When ICE finishes, a controlling agent MUST use the regular selection algorithm, and each agent SHOULD close all TCP connections it opened for ICE except those of the selected pairs. Aggressive selection could cause a connection to be closed just as it is chosen.

On a restart, agents MUST NOT close connections for selected pairs, and may offer an S-O candidate matching the old pair so the existing connection is reused. Connections to a STUN server SHOULD be closed after ICE completes. A connection to a TURN server MUST be kept open for the media session if a relayed candidate was selected. If a selected connection closes, an active or S-O side MUST reopen it, while a passive side waits.
sections.eli5: Pairs of doors are tried in order of how good they look. When one works, the others are closed and the working one stays open.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Media
sections.content:
If the selected pair matches an existing TCP connection, that connection MUST carry the media, and RFC 4571 framing MUST be used. For streams that are not RTP, the agent treats the stream as bytes, cuts it into arbitrary-length payloads, and wraps each in a frame with a length.

Before sending, the sender checks whether the bytes would look like a STUN message (the top two bits, the magic cookie, the length and the fingerprint). If they would, it MUST pick a different number of bytes so the length check fails. This is unlikely but possible, for example if a file transfer contains STUN messages.

The receiver extracts each frame's payload, decides whether it is STUN or application data, and appends non-STUN data to a byte stream it parses as if received directly from TCP. TLS or DTLS-SRTP handshakes run on top of the same shim, starting once media is permitted to flow. With SRTP, the RFC recommends running SRTP over the ICE connection rather than RTP over TLS.
sections.eli5: Messages go in labeled envelopes so the receiver can tell the ICE notes from the real content and put the content back together.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main threat is hijacking of connections to direct media at a denial-of-service target or a malicious user. With full implementations, ICE TCP only uses validated connections, and validation needs a STUN transaction that requires a shared secret exchanged in the rendezvous protocol, such as SIP. Using SIPS is RECOMMENDED. If that exchange is compromised, an attacker may fake validation, so additional mechanisms such as application-layer security are RECOMMENDED.

The STUN amplification attack from RFC 5245 applies, and is larger with TCP because a connection must be set up first. An agent SHOULD NOT have more than 5 outstanding TCP connection attempts with the same peer to the same IP address.

If both agents use lite mode, no checks are sent, so the connection is not validated unless media-level security is used. A peer behind a NAT might accidentally connect to a host in another subnet using the same private address space, which is one reason lite mode is not appropriate behind a NAT.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a door, each side has to say a secret password. If only one side is using the simple method, there is no password check, so be careful.

sections.title: Limitations of ICE TCP
sections.content:
Appendix A says ICE TCP generally has a lower chance than UDP-based ICE of connecting without a relay when both hosts are behind NATs. Many deployed NATs have endpoint-dependent mapping, or mishandle the packets of TCP simultaneous-open. A 2005 measurement cited in the RFC found simultaneous-open worked in roughly 45% of cases, and not all operating systems implement it properly.

Appendix B explains that standard BSD sockets are built for either initiating or receiving connections, so the code to do both on the same local address and port is non-obvious. All sockets for outgoing connections must be created and bound with SO_REUSEADDR before listen() is called, and the RFC's worst-case example gives MAX=25.

The RFC also includes IANA registration of a TCP token in a new ICE Transport Protocols sub-registry.
sections.eli5: The backup way is not as good, because many network gadgets handle it badly, and the programming is tricky too.
